reference_answer:
The literal task is to delineate scope, so neither continuity nor a scalar field may be silently inherited from a source convention. Separate: finite-group algebraic representation theory; continuous finite-dimensional real/complex representations of compact Hausdorff groups; and strongly continuous unitary representations on complex Hilbert spaces, with irreducibility there meaning NONZERO and no proper nonzero CLOSED invariant subspace. The complex matrix-coefficient/character statements below are explicitly complex statements. They are not claims about arbitrary fields or every abstract representation of the underlying compact group. Existence/uniqueness of normalized regular Haar measure is used as an EXTERNAL_THEOREM (source3.39), not proved here. On a compact group it is both left- and right-invariant, of total mass1. On a finite discrete group each point has mass1/|G|; ordinary unnormalized counting measure has mass|G|, so normalization must not be dropped.

(a) For a continuous finite-dimensional complex representation rho of compact Hausdorff G, fix any Hermitian metric h and define h_G(v,w)=integral h(rho(g)v,rho(g)w) dg. The integrand is continuous on a compact space, so this finite-dimensional entrywise integral exists. For v!=0 its squared norm is positive at the identity and hence bounded below by a positive number on a nonempty open neighborhood. Such a neighborhood has positive Haar measure: finitely many translates cover G, so measure0 would contradict total mass1. Thus h_G is positive definite. Right invariance gives h_G(rho(a)v,rho(a)w)=h_G(v,w). If W is invariant and v is h_G-orthogonal to W, then h_G(rho(a)v,w)=h_G(v,rho(a)^(-1)w)=0. Consequently V=W direct-sum W^perp as invariant subspaces. Induction on the finite dimension gives a FINITE algebraic direct sum of irreducibles. The same argument over R uses a real positive inner product. Zero V gives the empty sum; no nonzero irrep is inferred.

For an already unitary Hilbert representation, CLOSED W has the invariant orthogonal complement W^perp immediately, without averaging a new metric. Closedness and Hilbert completeness matter to the decomposition H=W orthogonal-sum W^perp. Finite-dimensional induction does not prove an infinite-dimensional algebraic decomposition. The compact-unitary Hilbert direct-sum theorem is an external Peter-Weyl representation theorem/corollary, not a consequence established here just by replacing a finite sum. In particular, it must not be promoted to an assertion about every invariant algebraic subspace or every normed/abstract representation.

Continuity is a real boundary, even in complex dimension2. Choose irrational alpha and a Q-linear map f:R->R with f(1)=0 and f(alpha)=1, by extending {1,alpha} to a Hamel basis. Then a(x+Z)=f(x) is a well-defined additive map R/Z->R. It is unbounded since a(n alpha+Z)=n, and hence not continuous on the compact circle. The abstract action rho(t)=[[1,a(t)],[0,1]] is a complex-linear invertible representation. The line Ce1 is invariant. Any complementary line has a vector e2+c e1; its image is e2+(c+a(t))e1. Invariance would force a(t)=0 for every t, a contradiction. Thus the unrestricted compact-as-an-abstract-group complement/completely-reducible claim fails. No measurability or integrability of this discontinuous action is assumed. Compactness alone does not justify the displayed integral.

The finite-group comparison is different. Over any field F with |G| invertible, choose a linear projection P onto invariant W and set Q=(1/|G|)sum rho(g)P rho(g)^(-1). Each summand has image in W and fixes W, so Q has image W and Q|W=I; conjugating the sum shows Q commutes with the action. Hence ker Q is an invariant complement. This needs no topology or positive metric. In finite dimension induction gives Maschke. If char F=p divides |G|, the average may be undefined and the conclusion can fail: C_p acts on F_p^2 by J=I+E12, since J^p=I, while the invariant line F_p e1 has no invariant complementary line. Thus the complex compact result is not a field-independent 'verbatim' extension of every modular statement.

(b) For a finite group, any NONZERO algebraically irreducible representation, even initially allowed an arbitrary-dimensional carrier, is finite-dimensional: for v!=0, span{rho(g)v:g in G} is a nonzero invariant space of dimension at most|G| and therefore equals V. For an infinite compact Hausdorff group, the properly scoped assertion is that every irreducible STRONGLY CONTINUOUS UNITARY representation on a complex Hilbert space is finite-dimensional. This is an EXTERNAL_THEOREM of compact representation theory/Peter-Weyl, not proved by the averaged metric. In a question that already restricts to finite-dimensional representations, finite-dimensionality is merely part of the typing, not a new conclusion. No unrestricted algebraic or discontinuous-irrep classification is claimed here.

Character orthogonality and the necessary coefficient normalization can be proved independently of Peter-Weyl completeness. Let rho,sigma be nonzero continuous finite-dimensional complex unitary irreps, with orthonormal bases. For X:V_sigma->V_rho, define T_X=integral rho(g)X sigma(g)^dagger dg. Haar invariance makes T_X an intertwiner. Schur's elementary kernel/image argument makes it0 for inequivalent irreps; for the same chosen irrep it is scalar, since a complex finite-dimensional endomorphism has an eigenvalue and its corresponding invariant kernel is the whole irreducible space. Trace gives T_X=(tr X/d_rho)I. Taking X a matrix unit yields integral conjugate(rho_ij(g))*sigma_kl(g) dg = delta_(rho,sigma)*delta_(i,k)*delta_(j,l)/d_rho, for a fixed set of inequivalent representatives. Summing diagonal indices gives integral conjugate(chi_rho)*chi_sigma=delta_(rho,sigma). Characters need NO sqrt(d_rho) factor, whereas the orthonormal coefficient functions are sqrt(d_rho)*rho_ij, not the raw entries.

The failure of raw normalization has a concrete witness. In the defining irreducible U(2) representation, Haar invariance under a row swap equates the integrals of |U11|^2 and |U21|^2, while a unit column makes their sum1. Thus the raw U11 coefficient has squared L2 norm1/2. This representation really is irreducible, because the unitary orbit of any nonzero vector spans C^2. Source3.42's unqualified raw-coefficient ON wording therefore needs this dimension normalization; matching source bytes would not repair the assertion.

(c) Invoke precisely the EXTERNAL Peter-Weyl density/completeness theorem for compact Hausdorff G: finite-dimensional continuous unitary matrix coefficients have dense span in complex L2(G,dg). Combining this theorem, not an elementary averaging proof of it, with the orthogonality just proved makes {sqrt(d_rho)*rho_ij} a Hilbert orthonormal basis. With left regular action L_h F(g)=F(h^(-1)g), one can identify L2(G) with the HILBERT direct sum over rho of V_rho tensor C^(d_rho). To get the displayed rho rather than its dual on the first factor, map e_i tensor e_j to sqrt(d_rho)*conjugate(rho_ij(g)): L_h of this function equals sum_k rho(h)_(k,i) times the corresponding k,j function. If raw rather than conjugated coefficient functions are used, fixed-column spans carry rho^*; relabeling the complete dual-closed irrep set gives the same multiplicity d_rho. This orientation choice is explicit.

The Hilbert sum consists of square-summable families and includes L2 limits, not only finite algebraic sums. The algebraic span of coefficients is dense but, for infinite G, generally proper. Infinite compact Hausdorff G has infinite-dimensional L2: for arbitrarily large m choose m disjoint nonempty open neighborhoods of distinct points; their positive-measure indicators are nonzero pairwise orthogonal vectors. No second-countability assumption is needed for this argument, and an arbitrary compact group need not have a countable coefficient basis. On the circle, the characters z^n (n in Z) give the familiar countable Hilbert Fourier basis, but an L2 function with infinitely many nonzero Fourier coefficients is not a finite algebraic sum. Continuous circle characters are exactly these integer powers: locally lifting a character to a real logarithm makes its lifted homomorphism linear by continuity, and period1 forces an integer slope.

For finite complex G, the regular character is|G| at the identity and0 elsewhere, so the multiplicity of rho is the normalized character inner product d_rho. Its finite-dimensional regular representation then gives sum_rho d_rho^2=|G|. For infinite compact G, keep multiplicity d_rho in the Hilbert regular decomposition; do NOT retain the finite real-number dimension equation, divide by an infinite cardinal, or mistake algebraic Hamel dimension for Hilbert dimension. For the circle, Hilbert dimension is countably infinite but |G| is continuum; an accidental cardinal equality with some different dimension convention is not the original finite identity. Likewise the circle has countably many continuous irreducible characters but continuum many singleton conjugacy classes, so the finite conjugacy-class count is not a literal compact extension.

Complex scope is essential to these particular character/degree-square formulas. For example, over R the trivial representation and the irreducible two-dimensional rotation representation of C_3 have squared real degrees summing1+4=5, not3; the latter has no real invariant line because a120-degree rotation has no real eigenvalue. This does not refute the complex finite formula. Compact Haar averaging over real/complex continuous finite-dimensional carriers, Schur orthogonality, external Peter-Weyl completeness, algebraic versus Hilbert sums and modular/exterior failures are separate layers. The notes refer to Knapp for Peter-Weyl; that proof was not inspected or reproduced. No local Lean closure, global alias/split decision, efficient Haar/circuit implementation or finite-bit resource bound follows from this delineation.
